Pilot hydrogen is used for the ignition of gaseous ethylene to improve combustion efficiency at low flight Mach numbers.
The process of dynamic flame stabilization has been investigated experimentally in a scramjet equipped with a cavity.

A variety of fuel injection strategies involving the injection of pure hydrogen, pure ethylene, and combinations of fuels were used to understand the effects of pilot hydrogen on supersonic combustion.

Experiments were conducted to investigate the effects of pilot hydrogen on the performance of an ethylene-fueled scramjet equipped with a single cavity.
The direct-connected CARDC facility was used to simulate a Mach number of 4 in flight conditions.
Optical measurements were performed using schlieren images, OH-PLIF, CH luminosity images, and 10 kHz pressure transducers.

The internal flow oscillated with a dominant frequency of approximately 450 Hz.
Specific injection strategies can be used to suppress oscillations in internal flow.
The experimental results showed that the high dominant frequency decreased when pilot hydrogen was injected into the cavity.
No significant impact on oscillation was noted when pilot hydrogen was injected ahead of the cavity step.
A reasonable injection strategy can reduce instability and improve the performance of the scramjet.

The ethylene flame remained stable when the pilot hydrogen was turned off.

Data clustering methods can be divided into three categories: distance-based methods, density-based methods, and connectivity-based methods.
Distance-based methods attempt to find relationships between data points based on various distance metrics.
Examples of distance-based methods include K-means (Wang et al. 2012, 2015) and agglomerative clustering (Chidananda Gowda and Krishna 1978).
Density-based methods attempt to cluster data points by appropriate density functions.
An example of a density-based method is density-based spatial clustering with noise (Wang et al. 2015).
Connectivity-based methods cluster data points into a cluster if they are highly connected.
A commonly used connectivity-based method is spectral clustering (Zelnik-Manor and Perona 2004).
The ideas of distance-based, density-based, and connectivity-based methods form the basis of many other methods.
Examples of methods based on these ideas include ensemble clustering (Huang et al. 2016) and clustering based on non-negative matrix factorization (Cai et al. 2009).

TemporalFlowViz is a visual analytics workflow and system for expert-guided exploration, clustering, and interpretation of temporal flow-field data from scramjet combustion simulations.

TemporalFlowViz combines ViT embeddings, interactive trajectory construction, density-based clustering, and expert-augmented semantic summarization to support interpretable analysis of high-dimensional, time-sequenced combustion data.
Experts can annotate representative cluster centroids, which condition a vision–language model for generating frame- and case-level descriptions.
This process establishes a reusable semantic layer that transforms complex flow field patterns into interpretable textual narratives.
The multimodal annotation pipeline enables automated reporting, similarity-driven retrieval, and collaborative analysis with minimal manual overhead.
The utility of TemporalFlowViz was demonstrated through two expert-driven case studies focusing on pressure and OH field dynamics.
The case studies revealed the system’s ability to distinguish combustion modes, uncover evolution patterns, and support scalable interpretation across parameterized simulations.
Expert feedback confirmed that the system accelerates hypothesis validation, reduces cognitive load, and facilitates knowledge sharing across teams.
TemporalFlowViz represents a step toward deeply integrated, expert-informed visual analytics for scientific simulations.
The system fuses deep learning, trajectory-based reasoning, and semantic interpretability into a unified framework for understanding combustion dynamics at scale.

A domain-adaptive Vision Transformer will be constructed through fine-tuning on large-scale combustion simulation datasets.
Fine-tuning on large-scale combustion simulation datasets will enhance the sensitivity of embeddings to subtle physical structures such as ignition fronts and weak flame zones.

The multimodal annotation workflow will reduce expert workload and help surface recurring knowledge patterns across large simulation corpora.
